stances.claim: China contests Scarborough and the Spratlys because they are in shallower waters suitable for mineral extraction and military construction; it concedes Benham Rise because it is outside the nine-dash line and too deep to be economically viable.
The arbitral tribunal had no jurisdiction over land sovereignty -- it could not award title or sovereignty over land territory, so China cannot be expected to surrender its occupation.
China's 2009 Note to the UNSG contested only Scarborough and Kalayaan -- implicitly conceding our rights over the Philippine archipelago and its corresponding Unclos zones including Benham Rise.
Deng Xiaoping's 1975 advice to Marcos -- 'talk some more, and more until agreement is reached' -- is consistent with and validates Duterte's Code of Conduct negotiation strategy.

one_paragraph_summary: Panganiban explains why China passionately contests Scarborough Shoal and the Spratlys but easily concedes Philippine rights over Benham Rise: Benham Rise is outside the nine-dash line and totally submerged (50-5,000 meters), making resource exploitation prohibitively expensive; the Spratlys and Scarborough are in shallower water where China has built airports, seaports, and military structures. Drawing on Estelito Mendoza's UP Law Center primer, he recounts the UNCLOS delegation's insider story: Mendoza and Jose Ingles as vice chairs (alternating chairs: Sen. Arturo Tolentino and Justice Secretary Vicente Abad Santos, all now deceased) convinced more numerous coastal states to accept archipelagic principles and the 200-NM EEZ as the 'ultimate compromise' far exceeding Hugo Grotius's 3-mile limit. RA 9522 (March 10, 2009) defined the baselines; China's April 13, 2009 Note to the UNSG contested only Scarborough and the Kalayaan Group but not the Philippine archipelago -- implicitly conceding our Unclos rights including over Benham Rise. The arbitral tribunal had no jurisdiction over land sovereignty and could not evict China from the features it occupies. Mendoza recalled Deng Xiaoping telling Marcos in June 1975 that if no agreement is reached, the solution is simply 'to talk some more, and more until agreement is reached' -- a prescription Duterte's Code of Conduct negotiations follow. The column closes with the open question: Is the Code of Conduct strategy a better approach to resolving the SCS impasse?
